summary: Epsilon Indi B is a known pair of brown dwarfs, objects too small to be stars, orbiting the star Epsilon Indi 12.1 light-years away. From 2010 to 2026 WANDERERS saw it move 74 arcseconds, 4.69 per year, matching Gaia's 4.68 within 0.2%. It is 2.5 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than in the 3.3 micron methane band, a sign of a cold, methane-rich atmosphere. Confidence is high, though 69 of 180 spectrum points are flagged and it brightened slightly (0.06 ± 0.03 mag), failing the steady-brightness check.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: It moves fast: 74 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, or 4.69 arcseconds per year. That matches Gaia DR3's 4.68 to within 0.2%, which shows it's the known object, 12.1 light-years away. It's also 2.5 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3 microns, where methane absorbs light. That pattern marks a cold brown dwarf. Caveats: its brightness changed by -0.06 ± 0.03 mag, and 69 of 180 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Over a third of the spectrum points (69 of 180) are flagged, so the spectrum's shape is less certain than the motion. The brightness changed by -0.06 ± 0.03 mag, only about twice its uncertainty, so that change may not be real. This is a pair of brown dwarfs, so SPHEREx sees their light blended together. I would be much less sure if the speed stopped matching Gaia or the methane ratio fell below 1.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: Time is the key. WISE photographed this sky in 2010 and SPHEREx in 2026, so together they give a 16-year baseline. Over that time Epsilon Indi B moved 74 arcseconds, about 12 SPHEREx pixels, which is easy to measure. SPHEREx's own visits span only about a year, under one pixel of motion. SPHEREx also adds a spectrum in many colors, revealing the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf.
